lead: Euler's formula assumes the material is linear elastic all the way to buckling. That holds only while the stress is below the proportional limit. On a short or intermediate aircraft strut the stress can pass this limit first, and the material is then softer: its tangent stiffness E<sub>t</sub> is less than Young's modulus E. The column buckles below the Euler load. This chapter gives the tangent-modulus and reduced-modulus loads, Shanley's correction, and Johnson's parabola for design checks of intermediate columns.
prereq: You need: Euler buckling of columns and end conditions for PE = π²EI/Le² and end conditions, and Rankine-Gordon formula for intermediate columns for the slenderness ratio λ = Le/r.

blocks.text: Slenderness is λ = Le/r, the effective length over the radius of gyration, as in Euler buckling. Two limiting values of λ appear in this chapter: λp, where the Euler stress reaches the proportional limit, and λJ, where Johnson’s parabola meets Euler’s curve.

The proportional limit σ<sub>prop</sub> is the highest stress at which the stress-strain curve is still a straight line. Below σ<sub>prop</sub> the slope is Young's modulus E. Above it, the slope falls and the material is partly plastic.

At a working stress σ, the tangent modulus E<sub>t</sub> is the slope dσ/dε of the stress-strain curve at that point. It is not a constant: E<sub>t</sub> = E below σ<sub>prop</sub> and E<sub>t</sub> < E above it. Engesser's idea is simple: a column buckles by bending, and bending stiffness depends on the current slope, not on the original E.

blocks.where: P<sub>cr</sub> is the inelastic buckling load (N); E<sub>t</sub> is the tangent modulus at the buckling stress (N/mm²); I is the least second moment of area (mm⁴); L<sub>e</sub> is the effective length (mm).

blocks.text: The switch from Euler to tangent modulus occurs at the proportional-limit slenderness λ<sub>p</sub>. Set the Euler stress π²E/λ² equal to σ<sub>prop</sub> and solve for λ.

blocks.where: λ<sub>p</sub> is the proportional-limit slenderness (dimensionless); E is Young's modulus (N/mm²); σ<sub>prop</sub> is the proportional limit (N/mm²).

blocks.text: For λ ≥ λ<sub>p</sub>, Euler is valid: σ<sub>cr</sub> = π²E/λ². For λ < λ<sub>p</sub>, the column is inelastic and Euler overpredicts the strength. In design, find λ first, compare with λ<sub>p</sub>, and only then choose the formula.

Kármán refined Engesser's model. When a column bows, the concave side is compressed further and loads along the tangent slope E<sub>t</sub>, while the convex side unloads elastically with slope E. The bending stiffness is therefore a weighted value called the reduced modulus E<sub>r</sub>, with E<sub>t</sub> < E<sub>r</sub> < E for a real metal. Kármán's load is P<sub>cr</sub> = π² E<sub>r</sub> I / L<sub>e</sub>², where E<sub>r</sub> replaces E<sub>t</sub> in the same formula.

Shanley settled which modulus starts the buckle. On a rising load path, a perfect column first becomes unstable at the tangent-modulus load P<sub>t</sub> = π²E<sub>t</sub> I/L<sub>e</sub>². It can then carry more load while bending grows, approaching the reduced-modulus load P<sub>r</sub>. The true bifurcation is at E<sub>t</sub>; E<sub>r</sub> is an upper bound for a perfect column and is not the load at which real columns first buckle.

For design, the conservative and simple choice is E<sub>t</sub>. Careful column tests gave strengths between the tangent-modulus and reduced-modulus values, usually close to the tangent value. Shanley’s load-path argument explained why: buckling starts at the tangent-modulus load and the extra strength appears only as bending grows.

If the stress-strain curve is known, read E<sub>t</sub> at the stress you expect, then solve P<sub>cr</sub> = π²E<sub>t</sub> I/L<sub>e</sub>² by trial, because E<sub>t</sub> depends on the stress. Handbooks give E<sub>t</sub> columns for aluminium and steel.
Johnson's parabolic formula is a closed-form fit for intermediate columns. It uses only σ<sub>y</sub> and E, so it is easy for hand calculations.

blocks.where: σ<sub>cr</sub> is the buckling stress (N/mm²); σ<sub>y</sub> is the yield strength (N/mm²); E is Young's modulus (N/mm²); λ = L<sub>e</sub>/r is the slenderness ratio (dimensionless).

blocks.text: It is valid up to λ<sub>J</sub> = √(2π²E/σ<sub>y</sub>). At that point σ<sub>cr</sub> = σ<sub>y</sub>/2. The parabola and Euler's hyperbola meet there with the same value, so the two curves join smoothly. Above λ<sub>J</sub>, use Euler.

For very short members, another failure comes first. A thin-walled angle or a flange buckles locally, or the cross-section cripples, at a stress below the column formula. Those are local-buckling and crippling checks made separately; do not use Johnson blindly for a short thin-walled strut.

figure.caption: Column curve for the aluminium alloy of the worked example (E = 70 GPa, σ<sub>Y</sub> = 320 MPa). Johnson’s parabola (solid, left) holds up to λ<sub>J</sub> = 65.7, where it meets Euler’s curve at σ<sub>Y</sub>/2 = 160 MPa; Euler (solid, right) holds above it. At λ = 40 the strut buckles at 260.7 MPa, while Euler (dashed, not valid) would give 431.8 MPa.

spec.aria: Buckling stress against slenderness from 0 to 120. A dashed line at the 320 megapascal yield strength. The Johnson parabola falls from 320 at zero slenderness to 160 at slenderness 65.7, where it touches the Euler hyperbola, which continues as a solid curve to the right and is dashed to the left where it is not valid. Points mark the example at slenderness 40: Johnson 260.7 and Euler 431.8, not valid.

examples.question: An aluminium alloy strut has E = 70 GPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = 320 MPa, A = 300 mm² and r = 5 mm. It is pinned at both ends with L = 0.20 m. Find the buckling stress and load, and compare with Euler.
steps: Convert the length: L = 0.20 m = 200 mm. For pinned ends, L<sub>e</sub> = L = 200 mm.
Johnson transition slenderness: λ<sub>J</sub> = √(2π²E/σ<sub>y</sub>). Use E = 70 GPa = 70 000 N/mm². 2π²E = 2 × 9.8696 × 70 000 = 1 381 744 MPa; divide by 320: 4317.95; √4317.95 = 65.7.
Since λ = 40.0 < 65.7, the column is inelastic. Euler is invalid.
Johnson stress: σ<sub>cr</sub> = σ<sub>y</sub> − cλ² = 320 − 0.03706 × 40² = 320 − 59.3 = 260.7 MPa.
Euler check: σ<sub>E</sub> = π²E/λ² = 690 870/1600 = 431.8 MPa. That is above the 320 MPa yield strength, so it is certainly above the proportional limit, and Euler does not apply.
examples.answer: The Johnson buckling stress is 260.7 MPa and the buckling load is 78.2 kN; Euler would wrongly give 431.8 MPa.
examples.check:
import math
E = 70000.0
sy = 320.0
A = 300.0
r = 5.0
L = 200.0
lam = L / r
lam<sub>t</sub> = math.sqrt(2 * math.pi**2 * E / sy)
c = sy**2 / (4 * math.pi**2 * E)
sig = sy - c * lam**2
P = sig * A / 1000
euler = math.pi**2 * E / lam**2
print(f"{lam:.1f}")
print(f"{lam<sub>t</sub>:.1f}")
print(f"{c:.5f}")
print(f"{sig:.1f}")
print(f"{P:.1f}")
print(f"{euler:.1f}")

traps: Using Euler when λ < λ<sub>p</sub>: Euler gives a stress above the proportional limit and is invalid.
Quoting Kármán's E<sub>r</sub> as the modulus that starts the buckle. Shanley's result is that E<sub>t</sub> starts it; E<sub>r</sub> is an upper bound.
Mixing L in metres with r in millimetres. Convert both to the same unit before computing λ.
Using σ<sub>y</sub> in place of σ<sub>prop</sub> to find λ<sub>p</sub> for Euler validity. The proportional limit is the correct cut-off.
Applying Johnson above λ<sub>J</sub>. The parabola is only valid up to λ<sub>J</sub>; above it use Euler.

quiz.q: Define proportional limit and tangent modulus.
quiz.a: The proportional limit is the highest stress on the straight part of the stress-strain curve. The tangent modulus E<sub>t</sub> is the slope dσ/dε at the working stress; it equals E below the proportional limit and is smaller above it.

quiz.q: Why does Euler's formula overpredict the strength of an intermediate column?
quiz.a: Because the working stress exceeds the proportional limit, so the material stiffness in bending is E<sub>t</sub> < E. Euler uses the full E and therefore predicts a higher buckling stress than the column can carry.

quiz.q: For the same aluminium alloy, E = 70 GPa and σ<sub>y</sub> = 320 MPa, find the Johnson buckling stress at λ = 50.
Explain why Shanley's tangent-modulus load is lower than Kármán's reduced-modulus load.
quiz.a: Kármán lets the convex side unload elastically with E while the concave side loads with E<sub>t</sub>, so E<sub>r</sub> > E<sub>t</sub>. Shanley showed that on a rising load path the first bifurcation happens while the whole section is still loading, so E<sub>t</sub> governs; the extra capacity from elastic unloading appears only after bending has grown.

quiz.q: State the Johnson transition slenderness λ<sub>J</sub> that separates Johnson’s parabola from Euler’s hyperbola.
quiz.a: λ<sub>J</sub> = √(2π²E/σ<sub>y</sub>). At this slenderness both formulas give σ<sub>y</sub>/2.

quiz.q: A material has E = 70 GPa and σ<sub>prop</sub> = 250 MPa. Find the proportional-limit slenderness λ<sub>p</sub> for Euler validity.
A very short thin-walled angle has λ = 30 and σ<sub>y</sub> = 320 MPa. Johnson predicts 286.6 MPa. Why may the real member fail earlier?
quiz.a: A thin wall can buckle locally or the section can cripple before the whole column reaches the Johnson stress. The column formula assumes the cross-section keeps its shape; local buckling violates that assumption.

quiz.q: A pinned strut has L = 1.2 m, r = 12 mm, E = 70 GPa and σ<sub>y</sub> = 320 MPa. Choose the valid formula and find σ<sub>cr</sub>.
quiz.a: λ = 1200/12 = 100. λ<sub>J</sub> = √(2π² × 70 000/320) = 65.7. Since λ > λ<sub>J</sub>, use Euler: σ<sub>cr</sub> = π²E/λ² = 690 870/10 000 = 69.1 MPa.

beyond: Not for the exam. In aircraft design, inelastic column curves are used for struts that are short enough to yield before they bow, and for thermal cases where aluminium alloys lose both E and σ<sub>y</sub> at temperature. Shanley's insight, that buckling is a load-path phenomenon rather than a single material constant, leads to nonlinear finite-element buckling analyses that track E<sub>t</sub>. Search for tangent-modulus column, Shanley column theory and Johnson parabola.
